content: Miscarriage is a frequent complication during pregnancy, and it can arise from various causes. Poor dietary intake of vitamins has been linked to an increased risk of miscarriage. Therefore, providing vitamin supplements to women either before conception or during early pregnancy might help reduce the risk of miscarriage. This review aimed to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of vitamin supplementation in preventing spontaneous miscarriage. The review included 40 trials involving 276,820 women and 278,413 pregnancies. These trials assessed the effects of vitamin supplementation initiated before 20 weeks of gestation. Eight of these trials were cluster-randomized, contributing data for 217,726 women and 219,267 pregnancies. Approximately half of the trials were judged to have a low risk of bias in terms of random sequence generation and allocation concealment. Vitamin C Supplementation: There was no significant difference in the risk of total fetal loss between women receiving vitamin C (with or without vitamin E) and those receiving a placebo or no vitamin C (RR 1.14, 95% CI 0.92 to 1.40; high-quality evidence). Similarly, no differences were observed in the risk of early or late miscarriage (RR 0.90, 95% CI 0.65 to 1.26; moderate-quality evidence) or stillbirth (RR 1.31, 95% CI 0.97 to 1.76; moderate-quality evidence). Adverse effects of vitamin C supplementation were also not significantly different (RR 1.16, 95% CI 0.39 to 3.41; moderate-quality evidence). Vitamin A Supplementation: No significant differences were found in the risk of total fetal loss (RR 1.01, 95% CI 0.61 to 1.66; low-quality evidence), early or late miscarriage (RR 0.86, 95% CI 0.46 to 1.62; low-quality evidence), or stillbirth (RR 1.29, 95% CI 0.57 to 2.91; low-quality evidence) between women receiving vitamin A (plus iron and folate) and those receiving a placebo or no vitamin A. There was no evidence of differences in miscarriage risk between women receiving other combinations of vitamin A and those receiving a placebo or no vitamin A. Multivitamin Supplementation: Women receiving multivitamins plus iron and folic acid had a reduced risk of stillbirth compared to those receiving iron and folate alone (RR 0.92, 95% CI 0.85 to 0.99; high-quality evidence). Total fetal loss was lower in women given multivitamins without folic acid (RR 0.49, 95% CI 0.34 to 0.70; one trial, 907 women) and in those given multivitamins with or without vitamin A (RR 0.60, 95% CI 0.39 to 0.92; one trial, 1074 women). However, these findings were based on single trials with small sample sizes, and caution is needed in interpreting these results. No significant differences were observed in the risk of total fetal loss (RR 0.96, 95% CI 0.93 to 1.00; high-quality evidence) or early or late miscarriage (RR 0.98, 95% CI 0.94 to 1.03; moderate-quality evidence) between women receiving multivitamins plus iron and folic acid and those receiving iron and folate alone. Folic Acid Supplementation: There was no evidence of differences in the risk of total fetal loss, early or late miscarriage, stillbirth, or congenital malformations between women supplemented with folic acid (with or without multivitamins and/or iron) and those not receiving folic acid. Antioxidant Vitamin Supplementation: No significant differences were observed in the risk of early or late miscarriage between women receiving antioxidant vitamins and those in the low-antioxidant group (RR 1.12, 95% CI 0.24 to 5.29; one trial, 110 women). Authors' Conclusions: Vitamin supplementation, whether taken before pregnancy or during early pregnancy, does not appear to prevent miscarriage. However, evidence suggests that women receiving multivitamins plus iron and folic acid may have a reduced risk of stillbirth. There is insufficient evidence to determine the effects of different combinations of vitamins on miscarriage and related outcomes.
